### METHODS

#### Preprocessing of scRNA-seq data

FASTQ files for scRNA-seq samples from the Bi and He et al. cohort were obtained from dbGap (accession number phs002065.v1.p1)20. FASTQ files for scRNA-seq samples from the Braun et al. cohort were obtained from dbGap (accession number phs002252.v1.p1)21. FASTQ files for scRNA-seq samples from the Krishna et al. cohort were obtained from the Sequence Read Archive (accession number PRJNA705464)22.

Barcode processing, read alignment, and UMI counting were performed using the 10x Genomics Cell Ranger analysis pipeline v6.0.1. Reads were aligned to the human genome reference b37 with the GENCODE 30 annotation lifted over to GRCh3779. Confidently mapped, non-PCR duplicate reads were counted to generate a gene-barcode matrix for each sample.

To abrogate sample-to-sample technical variability arising from cell-free RNA profiles, we performed ambient RNA decontamination on each sample from the three cohorts using CellBender v0.2.080. Raw counts for each sample were provided as input to the remove-background module of CellBender. Remove-background was run on all samples using the “full” model, 150 training epochs, and 25,000 total droplets included. For each sample, the expected cells parameter was derived from the estimated number of cells from Cell Ranger, rounded up to the nearest hundred. All other remove-background parameters were kept as default.

We performed multiplet detection and removal on CellBender-cleaned counts matrices using Scrublet v0.2.181. For each sample, the expected doublet rate parameter was set to 0.1. Doublet score thresholds were then selected manually to separate putative singlet and neotypic doublet modes in the distribution of simulated doublet scores. Predicted doublets were subsequently removed from each sample, yielding singlet-only, ambient RNA-cleaned counts matrices for downstream analysis in the Seurat R package v4.2.082.

Prior to further quality control and cell type annotation, all samples (42 total) were merged into a single Seurat object. Genes detected in fewer than three cells across samples were removed. Cells with fewer than 200 features detected or 25% or more of counts from mitochondrially-encoded transcripts were also removed. Raw counts were then normalized using the default Seurat log-normalization method. The top 2000 variable genes were identified using mean-variance standardized feature values (FindVariableFeatures function in Seurat with selection.method = “vst”). Data were scaled and principal components analysis (PCA) was performed on the scaled data. To unify samples across cohorts, we performed integration using the Harmony R package v0.1.083 on the top 50 principal components (PCs), adjusting for cohort of origin and sample as covariates. The 50 Harmony-corrected dimensions were then used for unsupervised Louvain clustering and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP).

#### Identification of malignant cells

Malignant cells were identified using inferred copy number profiles and cluster-level expression of canonical RCC tumor marker genes. For each sample, cells passing quality control were subsetted from the integrated Seurat object and data were re-normalized and re-scaled following feature selection as described. PCA was performed on the scaled data and the top 30 PCs were used for Louvain clustering and UMAP. Louvain clusters were annotated as broad cell types based on a panel of canonical marker genes for immune, stromal, and tumor cells. We then performed InferCNV (https://github.com/broadinstitute/inferCNV) on each sample, using putative tumor and stromal clusters as observation groups and immune clusters as reference groups. Malignant clusters were identified in InferCNV outputs based on clear patterns of copy number gain or loss, as well as known CNV features of RCC such as chromosome 3p loss. For samples where one or more clusters showed substantial heterogeneity in inferred copy number profiles, we performed an additional iteration of subsetting, normalization, scaling, PCA, and clustering for cells in the clusters of interest to resolve further cell states. We then reran InferCNV for said samples incorporating these more granular states to arrive at malignant cell calls.

These InferCNV results were then cross-referenced with broad cell type calls performed on Louvain clusters in the full integrated dataset. One cluster in particular showed highly specific expression of RCC tumor marker genes such as CRYAB, CLU, NDUFA4L2, and CA9. Cells in this cluster constituted 97.47% of cells labeled via InferCNV as malignant. Thus, cancer cells were definitively called as the overlap between cells in this cluster and cells identified as malignant using copy number profiles from InferCNV. Additionally, we excluded from downstream analysis all cells in this cluster labeled by InferCNV as non-malignant, and all cells not in this cluster (immune and stromal) labeled by InferCNV as malignant.

#### Annotation of cell types and subtypes

Annotation of granular tumor, immune, and stromal cell subtypes was performed via iterations of subsetting, normalization, feature selection, scaling, PCA, Harmony integration, Louvain clustering, and differential expression analysis within broad cell types.

For example, to annotate lymphoid cell subtypes, we first subsetted the integrated data to Louvain clusters labeled broadly as T cell, NK-like T cell, NK, T-reg, B cell, and plasma cell based on canonical marker expression, as well as lymphoid cells from a mixed cluster comprised of cycling cells from different immune lineages. Clustering and differential expression analysis within this lymphoid subset allowed for the identification of more high resolution states, including multiple groups of CD8 T cells and T-helper cells, plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs), as well as groups of cells with low quality-control metrics and/or ambiguous marker gene expression. For this level of annotation, differential expression analysis was performed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (FindMarkers function in Seurat with method = “wilcox”) with Bonferroni correction for multiple hypothesis testing. Subsequent iterations of subsetting, for example to only CD8 T cells or only T-helper cells, further clarified granular cell states and enabled identification of low quality/ambiguous/contaminating cells. Lastly, to achieve cell subtype annotations without any influence of low quality/ambiguous/contaminating cells, we performed a final iteration of subsetting and clustering on each individual lymphoid cell type (CD8 T cell, T-helper, T-reg, NK, B and plasma cell), excluding poor quality cells. For this final level of annotation, differential expression analysis was performed using a logistic regression framework (FindMarkers function in Seurat with method = “LR”) with Bonferroni correction for multiple hypothesis testing. The highly granular annotations obtained via these subsetted objects were then mapped back onto the full integrated dataset and used to re-define broad cell types among high quality cells only.

We applied this approach to lymphoid and myeloid lineages, as well as stromal and tumor cells, resulting in a final set of 228,371 high quality total cells across 14 broad cell types (tumor, fibroblast, perivascular, endothelial, TAM, monocyte, DC, CD8 T cell, CD8 NK-like, NK, T-helper, T-reg, B cell, and plasma cell) (Table S1A).

#### Single cell signature scoring

All single cell signature scoring was performed on normalized data using the combined z-score approach (“zscore” method parameter) implemented by the hacksig R package v0.1.284,85.

#### Defining putative ISGs

Putative ISGs were defined as the union of genes from the HALLMARK_INTERFERON_GAMMA_RESPONSE and HALLMARK_INTERFERON_ALPHA_RESPONSE gene sets from MSigDB, the IFNG.GS and ISG.RS gene sets from Benci et al14, and a curated set of genes encoding inhibitory ligands, immune checkpoints, and other immune evasion factors with prior evidence for being regulated by IFN signaling (Table S1D).

#### Inferring IFN-inducibility of genes

To infer the IFN-inducibility of genes in our dataset, we first used CytoSig v126 to quantify relative type-I and type-II IFN signaling at single cell resolution within each cell type. For a given broad cell type, we provided a normalized, mean-centered expression matrix containing cells of that type and all genes in the dataset as input to CytoSig. Because fibroblasts and perivascular cells showed highly similar expression profiles in our data, these two cell types were combined into a single group for CytoSig scoring and IFN-inducibility inference. We ran CytoSig with default parameters to obtain scores for IFNα/β and IFNγ cytokine signaling activity in cells of each cell type. For later analyses requiring binning of cells into discrete IFNα/β or IFNγ signaling low and high groups, we considered cells with a CytoSig z-score > 0 and CytoSig p-value < 0.05 as signaling-high and cells with a CytoSig z-score < 0 and CytoSig p-value < 0.05 as signaling-low.

Next, for a given gene, we fit a linear mixed effects model within cells of a given broad cell type for predicting normalized expression using IFNα/β CytoSig score, IFNγ CytoSig score, number of genes detected per cell, early (I/II) versus late (III/IV) disease stage, and patient of origin as predictor variables. In these models, patient of origin was considered a random effect, and all other variables were considered fixed effects. Models were fit using the lmer function from the lmerTest R package v3.1.386. β coefficients for IFNα/β and IFNγ CytoSig scores in these models represent IFN inducibility, i.e. the extent to which relative type I and type II IFN signaling levels predict the expression of a given gene. We fit these models for all putative ISGs and a set of highly variable genes. Here, highly variable genes were defined as the union of the top 2000 most variable genes across all cell types and the top 2000 variable genes within each broad cell type as determined using the FindVariableFeatures function in Seurat with selection.method = “vst”. Across these mixed effects models, p-values for IFNα/β and IFNγ CytoSig scores were adjusted using Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction. Genes with an IFNα/β CytoSig score β coefficient > 0 and BH-adjusted p < 0.01 were considered type-I-inducible, while genes with an IFNγ CytoSig score β coefficient > 0 and BH-adjusted p < 0.01 were considered type-II-inducible.

We applied this approach for inferring the IFN-inducibility of genes within cell types using (a) the full integrated dataset (Table S2A-S2M) and (b) cells from previously untreated patients only, describing IFN-driven variability in gene expression at baseline before first-line therapy (Table S3A-S3M).

#### Determining sources of IFNs in RCC tumors

To identify cell types and subtypes contributing IFNγ to the RCC microenvironment, we applied multiple linear regression models to predict IFNγ signaling levels across samples using CD8, CD8 NK-like, and NK cell proportions and IFNG expression as explanatory variables (Figure S3B).

For a given broad cell type, we calculated the median IFNγ CytoSig score and median IFNα/β CytoSig score within each sample. We then fit a multiple linear regression model for predicting median IFNγ CytoSig scores using the proportion of CD8s, CD8 NK-like, and NK cells in each sample, the percentages of CD8s, CD8 NK-like, and NK cells in each sample expressing IFNG with greater than 0 normalized counts, and median IFNα/β CytoSig scores as predictor variables. We fit these regression models for each broad cell type in the dataset. Again, because fibroblasts and perivascular cells showed highly similar expression profiles in our data, these two cell types were combined into a single group for this analysis. Models were fit using the lm function from the base stats R package v4.1.0.

To pinpoint the source of IFNγ to granular CD8 subsets, we applied a similar modeling approach. Again, for a given broad cell type, we calculated the median IFNγ CytoSig score and median IFNα/β CytoSig score within each sample. We then fit a multiple linear regression for predicting median IFNγ CytoSig scores using the proportion of CD8 41BB-Hi, CD8 LAG3-Hi, CD8 HSP-Hi, CD8 ISG-Hi, and CD8 IL7R-Hi cells in each sample, the percentages of CD8 41BB-Hi, CD8 LAG3-Hi, CD8 HSP-Hi, CD8 ISG-Hi, and CD8 IL7R-Hi cells in each sample expressing IFNG with greater than 0 normalized counts, and median IFNα/β CytoSig scores as predictor variables. Cycling CD8 subsets (CD8 Cyc. 1, CD8 Cyc. 2, CD8 Cyc.4), subsets comprised primarily of cells from a single sample (CD8 TRBV5-6-Hi, CD8 TRBV3-1-Hi), subsets consisting of less than 2000 cells (CD8 KLRB1-Hi, CD8 FOXP3-Hi, CD8 TRBV7-7-Hi), and a subset with low nFeatures and nCounts per cell and defined by genes encoding ribosomal subunits (CD8 RPS-Hi) were not considered in this analysis. We again fit these regression models for each broad cell type in the dataset.

We then attempted to determine cell types contributing IFNα/β to the RCC microenvironment using a similar approach. For each broad cell type, we fit a multiple linear regression for predicting median IFNα/β CytoSig scores using the proportion of TAMs, monocytes, DCs, tumor cells, endothelial cells, and perivascular cells and fibroblasts, as well as median IFNγ CytoSig scores as predictor variables. In these models, tumor cell proportion appeared to consistently predict IFNα/β CytoSig scores across cell types. However, closer inspection of the data revealed that these results could be driven by samples from a single patient from the Krishna et al cohort (patient UT2). Upon omitting these samples and re-fitting our linear models, we found that no broad cell type proportion was consistently significantly predictive of type-I IFN signaling (Figure S3D-S3F).

#### Derivation of IFN signaling signatures

We defined gene signatures of cell type-specific type-I and type-II IFN signaling based on criteria for both cell type specificity and IFN inducibility using cells from ICB-naive patients only.

First, we established groups of broad cell types based on similar patterns of putative ISG expression. TAMs, monocytes, and DCs formed one group (myeloid), CD8, CD8 NK-like, NK, T-helper, and T-reg formed another (T/NK), and tumor cells and perivascular cells/fibroblasts formed a third group (tumor/fibroblast).

For a given broad cell type, we identified cell type-specific (CTS) genes by performing a series of pairwise one-versus-each differential expression tests between that cell type and all other cell types. Differential expression testing was performed using the FindMarkers function in Seurat with method = “LR”. Early (I/II) versus late (III/IV) disease stage and patient of origin were incorporated as latent variables; p-values were adjusted using Bonferroni correction. A gene was considered cell type-specific only if it passed the following cutoffs in all pairwise tests (excluding tests between cell types in the same group): average log2FC > 0, pctCOI - pctComp > 0, pctComp < 20, and Bonferroni adjusted p-value < 0.05. Here, pctCOI represents the percentage of cells in the cell type of interest expressing the gene at greater than 0 normalized counts, and pctComp represents the percentage of cells in the comparator cell type expressing the gene at greater than 0 normalized counts.

For each broad cell type, we then identified the overlap of CTS genes with significantly type-I or type-II-inducible putative ISGs in that cell type as determined by our mixed effects modeling approach in cells from ICB-naive patients. These CTS, significantly IFN-inducible genes were then combined across cell types of the same group to arrive at signatures of myeloid, T/NK, and tumor/fibroblast IFNα/β and IFNγ signaling (Figure S5C, Table S1D), which were then used for clinical outcomes analysis in IM151 and JR101.

TAM, monocyte, and DC non-IFN-inducible signatures were initially defined as CTS genes for which the abs(β coefficient) of both IFNα/β CytoSig score and IFNγ CytoSig score were < 0.1 and corresponding BH-adjusted p-value > 0.1. These signatures were then filtered to exclude genes with IFNα/β CytoSig score or IFNγ CytoSig score β coefficient > 0.1 and corresponding BH-adjusted p-value < 0.05 in any of the three myeloid cell types (TAM, monocyte, or DC).

#### Derivation of expanded IFN signaling signatures

The myeloid, T/NK, and tumor/fibroblast IFNα/β and IFNγ signaling signatures described above were constrained to our pre-defined set of 259 putative ISGs, primarily grounded in the highly canonical Hallmark IFNγ response and Hallmark IFNα response gene-sets. However, a more comprehensive set of putative ISGs can be derived from experimental datasets. We therefore expanded our set of putative ISGs using genes exhibiting consistent IFNγ or IFNα/β inducibility in the CytoSig treatment response database, then used this expanded set to re-identify cell type-specific ISG signatures using our same criteria for cell type specificity and interferon inducibility (Figure S10A-S10F). We then examined the association between these expanded signatures and ICB outcomes in IM151 and JR101 (Figure S10G-S10J).

First, we obtained the data matrix of cytokine treatment responses (weighted log2FC) and meta information for each treatment profile from the CytoSig web portal (https://cytosig.ccr.cancer.gov/)26. We then subsetted the treatment response data to either IFNγ-treated experiments or IFNα/β-treated experiments. For each experiment, we manually annotated the broad cell type of the tested cell model, and only considered experiments in broad cell types with relevance to our study (cell types such as neuroblastoma, and placenta were excluded, for example).

For IFNγ-treated experiments, we considered the following broad cell types: B cell, DC, macrophage, monocyte, endothelial, fibroblast, proximal tubule epithelial, melanoma, and lung adenocarcinoma. For IFNα/β-treated experiments, we considered the following cell types: B cell, DC, endothelial, fibroblast, macrophage, monocyte, T cell, melanoma, and lung adenocarcinoma. The inclusion of melanoma and lung adenocarcinoma cell lines for this analysis was intended to help retrieve additional tumor/epithelial-expressed ISGs. For each broad cell type, we then identified all genes with a weighted log2FC > 1.5 in greater than 50% of experiments within that broad cell type. Exceptions were made for broad cell types with just 2 or 3 experiments; for these, genes were retained if they had a weighted log2FC > 1.5 in greater than 1 experiment. We performed this analysis separately for IFNg-treated and IFNa/b-treated experiments. Under this approach, we identified 118 putative ISGs not present in our original 259-gene putative ISG set.

Using this expanded putative ISG set (377 genes total) (Table S1D), we re-derived myeloid, T/NK, and tumor/fibroblast IFN signaling signatures using the approach described above. The inclusion of these additional putative ISGs from CytoSig resulted in only a single new signature gene for tumor/fibroblasts (DSP, an IFNγ-inducible gene) and no new signature genes for T and NK cells (Figure S10A, S10B, Table S1D). However, several new IFNγ and IFNα/β signaling signature genes were identified for myeloid cells (Figure S10A, S10B, Table S1D). In myeloid cells, SLAMF8, PSTPIP2, and FCGR1B emerged as IFNg-only ISGs. IL1RN, C1QB, and SIGLEC1 emerged as IFNα/β-only ISGs. TNFSF13B, FPR2, and ANKRD22 emerged as both IFNγ-inducible and IFNα/β-inducible myeloid ISGs. These expanded signatures exhibited patterns of expression similar to our original signatures in single cell samples not used for signature discovery and in bulk RNA-seq data (Figure S10C-S10F).

We then asked whether these expanded signatures were predictive of immunotherapy outcomes in IM151 and JR101. Consistent with our original signatures, the myeloid IFNγ signaling expanded signature, but not the tumor/fibroblast IFNγ signaling expanded signature, was associated with poorer outcomes under ICB plus anti-VEGF in IM151 and JR101 (Figure S10G-S10J). Thus, models employing the expanded signatures still primarily implicate myeloid IFNγ signaling as a predictor of immunotherapy resistance, and do not drastically deviate from the results obtained using our original signatures. We provide both the original and expanded signatures for readers in Table S1D.

#### Bulk RNA-seq signature scoring and deconvolution

Raw sequencing data and associated clinical metadata for the JAVELIN Renal 101 cohort were obtained from published results63,64. Paired-end bulk RNA-seq samples were realigned to the hg19 genome reference using STAR v2.7.087, with alignment parameters --outFilterMultimapNmax 20 --outFilterMismatchNmax 999 --outFilterMismatchNoverReadLmax 0.04 --alignIntronMin 20 --alignIntronMax 1250000 --alignMatesGapMax 1250000. Sequencing primers were removed with cutadapt88, gene expression was quantified using RSEM89 v1.3.1, and duplicate reads were marked using Picard’s Mark Duplicates (https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/). Quality control metrics were extracted using RNA-SeQC290. For each sample, we obtained the number of genes detected (GD), the estimated library size, the end 1 sense rate (E1SR), the end 2 sense rate (E2SR) and exonic rate from RNA-SeQC2. For each sample, we also calculated the gene interquartile range (IQR) as previously described91 to estimate the dynamic range of gene expression. First, potential sample outliers in gene expression space were detected by PCA analysis of TPM-normalized expression values. We plotted the above quality metrics stratified by potential outliers versus potentially quality control passing samples, and were able to determine the most appropriate thresholds. The following thresholds provided the best outlier detection: GD ≤ 16000, geneIQRs ≤ 0, E2SR ≥ 0.1, E1SR ≤ 0.85.

Recurrent copy number variants (CNVs) in whole-exome sequencing samples from JAVELIN Renal 101 were determined using GISTIC2.092, v2.0.23, with the following input parameters: amplification threshold=0.1, deletion threshold=0.1, q-value threshold=0.1, cap values=1.5, broad length cutoff=0.7, confidence level=0.99, join segment size=20, arm level peel off=1, maximum sample segments=800, gene collapse method=mean, including matched normals as reference.

Processed bulk RNA-seq data and associated clinical metadata from the IMmotion151 cohort were obtained from published results (European Genome-Phenome Archive: EGAS00001004353)61,62.

All signature scoring in bulk RNA-seq data was performed on normalized TPM matrices using the combined z-score approach (“zscore” method parameter) implemented by the hacksig R package v0.1.284,85. Apart from signatures derived in this study, signatures describing various immune cell states and phenotypes were obtained from previously published studies17,22,64,67,69.

To infer cell type proportions in bulk RNA-seq samples, we performed deconvolution using CIBERSORTx Fractions via the CIBERSORTx docker and source code65. First, we constructed a reference using ICB-naive samples in our single cell data. We downsampled this subset of the data to a maximum of 3000 cells from each broad cell type. We then removed all genes encoding mitochondrial transcripts and ribosomal proteins (RPS and RPL genes), as well as genes with 0 total counts across the downsampled data. We ran CIBERSORTx Fractions using non-logged TPM matrices for the IMmotion151 and JAVELIN Renal 101 bulk RNA-seq data as mixture files, the downsampled, gene-filtered, non-logged single cell reference expression matrix as the refsample, S-mode batch correction, no quantile normalization, and 1 permutation (CIBERSORTx p-values were not used for downstream analysis).

#### Clinical outcomes analysis

Cox proportional hazards (PH) analysis and Kaplan-Meier analysis were performed using the survival v3.2.11 and survminer v0.4.9.999 R packages. To determine the relationship between baseline levels of cell type-specific IFN signaling and outcomes under first-line ICB plus anti-VEGF therapy, we fit multivariate Cox proportional hazards models for progression-free survival (PFS) in each treatment arm of IMmotion151 and JAVELIN Renal 101 using the coxph function. These models incorporated as predictor variables myeloid IFNγ or IFNα/β signaling signature score, tumor/fibroblast IFNγ or IFNα/β signaling signature score, Krishna CD8 predictive signature score, TAM, monocyte, DC, CD8, tumor cell, and fibroblast fractions as inferred by CIBERSORTx, as well as age, sex, MSKCC risk group, and PD-L1 positivity. All continuous variables were scaled in these models.

Further inspection of models fitted in the ICB plus anti-VEGF arms of both studies revealed mild violations of the proportional hazards assumption for some variables (determined using the cox.zph function of the survival R package). Schoenfeld residuals were visualized using the coxzphplot function of the autoReg R package v0.3.4. In a Cox model for PFS in the atezolizumab plus bevacizumab treatment arm of IMmotion151, MSKCC risk group, TAM fraction, and DC fraction showed statistically significant violation of the PH assumption (Table S4C). However, stratification of the model by MSKCC risk group using the strata function in the survival R package did not substantially affect the hazard ratio or associated p-value of key predictor variables (myeloid IFNγ signaling HR = 1.59, 95% C.I. = 1.21–2.09, p < 0.001; Krishna CD8 predictive HR = 0.51, 95% C.I. = 0.35-0.72, p < 0.001) (Table S4D, S4E). Removal of all cell type fractions from the stratified model (resolving all violations of the PH assumption) also had no substantial effect on the HR or p-value of these variables (myeloid IFNγ signaling HR = 1.66, 95% C.I. = 1.30-2.12, p < 0.001; Krishna CD8 predictive HR = 0.58, 95% C.I. = 0.45-0.75, p < 0.001) (Table S4F, S4G).

In a Cox model for PFS in the avelumab plus axitinib treatment arm of JAVELIN Renal 101, only patient age showed statistically significant violation of the PH assumption (Table S4H). Removal of age from the model (resolving all violations of the PH assumption) had no substantial effect on the HR or p-value of key variables (myeloid IFNγ signaling HR = 1.50, 95% C.I. = 1.03-2.17, p = 0.033; Krishna CD8 predictive HR = 0.56, 95% C.I. = 0.37-0.85, p = 0.007) (Table S4I, S4J).

For Kaplan-Meier analysis, optimal cutoffs for Krishna CD8 predictive and myeloid IFNγ signaling signatures were established using the surv_cutpoint function from the survminer R package with the minprop parameter set to 0. In the ICB plus anti-VEGF treatment arm of each study, we first applied surv_cutpoint on the Krishna CD8 predictive signature and defined samples as signature-low or signature-high based on the optimal threshold. Within Krishna CD8 predictive-high samples in the ICB plus anti-VEGF treatment arm, we then applied surv_cutpoint on the myeloid IFNγ signaling signature and defined samples as signature-low or signature-high based on the optimal threshold. These same thresholds were applied to the sunitinib treatment arm of each study. We then assessed the effect of myeloid IFNγ signaling on PFS as a categorical variable (high/low) in multivariate and univariate Cox models in each arm of the two studies. For multivariate analysis, predictor variables included myeloid IFNγ signaling as a categorical variable, TAM, monocyte, and DC fractions as inferred by CIBERSORTx, as well as age, sex, MSKCC risk group, and PD-L1 positivity. All continuous variables were scaled in these models.

Multivariate logistic regression analysis for predicting clinical benefit (CB) versus no clinical benefit (NCB) was performed using the glm function from the base stats R package v4.1.0 with the family parameter set to “binomial”. Patients with clinical benefit were defined as those with an objective response of CR, PR, or SD with PFS greater than or equal to 6 months. Patients with no clinical benefit were defined as those with an objective response of PD or SD with PFS less than 6 months. These logistic regression models incorporated as predictor variables myeloid IFNγ or IFNα/β signaling signature score, tumor/fibroblast IFNγ or IFNα/β signaling signature score, Krishna CD8 predictive signature score, TAM, monocyte, DC, CD8, tumor cell, and fibroblast fractions as inferred by CIBERSORTx, as well as age, sex, MSKCC risk group, and PD-L1 positivity. All continuous variables were scaled in these models.

To assess the effect of non-ISG or external myeloid signatures on clinical outcomes, we fit a series of multivariate Cox models for PFS and logistic regression models for CB versus NCB in the ICB plus anti-VEGF treatment arms of both studies. These models incorporated as predictor variables a given myeloid signature score, Krishna CD8 predictive signature score, tumor/fibroblast IFNγ signaling signature score, TAM, monocyte, DC, CD8, tumor cell, and fibroblast fractions as inferred by CIBERSORTx, as well as age, sex, MSKCC risk group, and PD-L1 positivity. All continuous variables were scaled in these models. The variance inflation factor (VIF) for each variable in these models was calculated using the car R package v3.1.1. Only models where the VIF of all variables was less than 10 were considered valid for this analysis.

#### NY-ESO-1 TCR transduction

We generated retrovirus encoding an NY-ESO-1–specific TCR (pMX vector harboring IRES-GFP) using a standard two-step packaging strategy and introduced it into human T cells, adapted from a published protocol93. First, Phoenix-GPE packaging cells were transfected with the vector using TransIT-LT1 (Mirus Bio, #MIR 2304). After 24 hours, the supernatant was collected. The filtered supernatant was then used to transduce PG13 cells in the presence of polybrene (MilliporeSigma, #TR-1003-G), with spin infection to enhance viral entry. Following a brief incubation, the medium was replaced with fresh complete medium, and PG13 cells were expanded to obtain virus-containing supernatant. Human T cells were isolated from cryopreserved healthy-donor PBMCs by negative selection using a biotinylated antibody cocktail and magnetic beads (Miltenyi Biotec, Pan T cell isolation kit, #130-096-535). Purified cells were resuspended in T-cell medium and activated with 20 IU/ml IL-2 (Miltenyi Biotec, #130-097-745). Activation was performed by seeding T cells into wells pre-coated with anti-CD3 antibody (Biolegend, #317325) and RetroNectin (Takara Bio USA, #T100B). For TCR transfer, PG13-derived viral supernatant was loaded onto plates pretreated with RetroNectin and anti-CD3 and centrifuged to adsorb virions to the substrate, after which pre-activated T cells were seeded onto the virus-bound plates. Spin introduction was applied and then cells were subsequently cultured at 37 °C in 5% CO2 in IL-2–supplemented medium. Transduction efficiency was assessed approximately one week later by flow-cytometric quantification of GFP positivity among live cells. For experiments using chronically stimulated T cells, cells were generated by once-daily stimulation for five consecutive days prior to use.

#### Stimulation of monocyte-derived macrophages

Human monocytes were isolated from healthy-donor PBMCs by positive selection using CD14 MicroBeads according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Miltenyi Biotec, CD14 MicroBeads, #130-050-201). Purified CD14 cells were cultured at 37 °C in 5% CO2 in RPMI medium supplemented with recombinant human M-CSF (50 ng/mL) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #PHC9504) to induce differentiation into monocyte-derived macrophages. Differentiation was continued until cells displayed adherent macrophage morphology within 7 days. The macrophage phenotype was verified by flow cytometry as CD11b+CD33+CD163+. For activation, differentiated macrophages were either left unstimulated (control) or primed with recombinant human IFN-γ (10 ng/mL) (Thermo Fisher Scientific, #PHC4031) for 24 h. Both unstimulated and IFN-γ-stimulated macrophages were subsequently used in the killing assays described below.

#### In vitro cytotoxicity assay

We tested cytotoxic activity using a luciferase assay as described previously94. To assess T-cell cytotoxicity, we established an antigen-specific killing assay using NY-ESO-1 (CTAG1B) as the model antigen. The human RCC cell lines UOK-127 and A498 (both HLA-A*02:01–positive) were used as target cells. The luciferase gene and CTAG1B gene (encoding NY-ESO-1) were introduced into cell lines using a lentivirus system, and T cells were engineered to express the NY-ESO-1–specific T cell receptor restricted by HLA-A*02:01 (NY-ESO-1 T cells) using a retroviral system as described above. In the killing assay, the genetically-engineered RCC cell lines (5.0 × 104 cells per well) were co-cultured with NY-ESO-1 T cells at 1:1 or 3:1 effector to target ratios and IFNγ-stimulated macrophages or unstimulated macrophages (1.5 × 105 cells), or no macrophages for 18 hours. To measure the cytotoxic activity of NY-ESO-1 T cells, a luciferase substrate (Promega, Bright-Glo™ Luciferase Assay System, #E2610) was directly added to each well. Emitted light was detected in a SpectraMax M3 (Molecular Devices). Lysis was determined as (1 – (RLUsample)/(RLUmax)) × 100.

Single cell suspensions from induced macrophages were blocked with Human TruStain FcX™ (Biolegend, #422302). Single cell suspensions from T cells were stained with the following anti-human antibodies and the brilliant stain buffer (BD Biosciences): BUV737-CD45 (HI30, #568524), BUV395-CD3 (UCHT1, #563546), BV786-TIM-3 (344823, #747958), and BV421-TIGIT (741182, #747844) were purchased from BD Bioscience. ### QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS

Statistical analyses were performed using R v4.1.0 and GraphPad Prism. Statistical details (including sample size n) are reported in results, figures, figure legends, STAR methods, supplementary tables, and data analysis code in the public repository for this study (see Data and Code Availability). Inclusion/exclusion criteria for cells, signatures, samples, and clinical groupings for all analyses are described in detail in results and relevant STAR Methods sections. For all figures, *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001.

Differential expression testing for initial cell type annotations was performed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (FindMarkers function in Seurat with method “wilcox”. Other differential expression analysis (final cell subset annotation, one-versus-each testing to identify CTS genes) was performed using a logistic regression framework and likelihood ratio test (FindMarkers function in Seurat with method = “LR”); early/late disease stage and patient were incorporated as latent variables and p-values were adjusted using Bonferroni correction. Significance testing for differences in signature scores between groups of cells or sample-level median scores between cell types was performed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. For all box plots, the centerline is the median, the box limits are upper and lower quartiles, and whiskers extend to the most extreme values within 1.5 times the interquartile range. Linear mixed effects models for inferring the IFN-inducibility of individual genes were fit using the lmer function of the lmerTest R package v3.1.3; p-values for the IFNα/β and IFNγ CytoSig score variables were adjusted across models using Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction. Multiple linear regression models for inferring median IFNα/β and IFNγ CytoSig scores as a function of cell type proportions were fitted using the lm function of the base stats R package v4.1.0. Significance testing for differences in TAM subtype frequencies between groups of samples was performed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Error bars represent mean ± SD.

Significance testing for differences in signature scores between groups of bulk RNA-seq samples was performed using a two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional-hazards models for progression-free survival were fit using the coxph function of the survival R package v3.2.11. Testing for violation of the proportional-hazards assumption in these models was performed using the cox.zph function of the survival R package and visualization of Schoenfeld residuals was performed using the coxzphplot function of the autoReg R package v0.3.4. Logistic regression models for predicting clinical benefit versus no clinical benefit were fit using the glm function of the base stats R package v4.1.0. Kaplan-Meier analysis was performed using the survfit and ggsurvplot functions, and optimal signature score cutoffs for stratification were determined using the surv_cutpoint function from the survminer R package v0.4.9.999.

Significance testing for differences in inhibitory ligand expression (mean fluorescence intensity) between IFNγ-stimulated and unstimulated macrophages was performed using a two-sided t-test. Error bars represent mean ± SEM. Significance testing for differences in lysis of RCC cells by T cells in co-culture with IFNγ-stimulated macrophages versus unstimulated macrophages was performed using a two-sided t-test. Values were normalized to lysis without macrophages. Error bars represent mean ± SEM.

## Abstract

Immune checkpoint inhibition can result in deep and durable responses in clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), yet no biomarkers currently guide management. While mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency is an established predictive biomarker for immunotherapy response in other malignancies, this has not been evaluated in ccRCC, despite the proximity of MMR gene MLH1 to VHL on chromosome 3p. Through genomic and immunohistochemical analyses across multiple cohorts, we identify somatic MLH1 deficiency as a relatively rare but robust predictor of exceptional immunotherapy response in ccRCC.

In patients with metastatic clear-cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) combination therapy outperforms vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) targeted monotherapy [1–3]. Doublet regimens combining programmed death 1 (PD-1) and either cytotoxic T-lymphocyte–associated antigen-4 (CTLA-4) or VEGF inhibition are established first-line therapies. Nonetheless, questions persist regarding optimal patient and regimen selection, with no biomarkers to guide management [4–6].

Mismatch repair (MMR), microsatellite instability (MSI), and tumor mutational burden (TMB) are approved as tumor-agnostic biomarkers for ICIs [7]. However, TMB has not demonstrated predictive value for ICI response in ccRCC [4–6]. A small but nontrivial portion of ccRCC cases harbor MMR gene alterations, but their relationship with ICIs remains unknown [8]. We investigated whether MMR deficiency predicts an exceptional ICI response in ccRCC, with implications for both metastatic and high-risk localized disease management, especially given the recent evidence for adjuvant pembrolizumab [9].

First, we reviewed 893 patients with ccRCC sequenced using the IMPACT panel in the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSK) clinical sequencing cohort, to establish the prevalence of MMR gene alterations (Fig. 1A). Among the 474 patients sequenced before receiving systemic therapy, 24 (5.1%) had loss-of-function MMR alterations. Five additional cases (1.1%) had wild-type MMR but were either MSI-high (MSIsensor >10) or TMB-high (>10 mutations/Mb). These were investigated due to potential epigenetic silencing, which causes MMR deficiency in other malignancies, but could not be detected with the available data [10].

Next, we evaluated which genomic alterations manifested as MMR protein deficiency. Specimens were available for immunohistochemical (IHC) staining in 16 of 29 cases (Fig. 1A). Only MLH1 had consistent congruence between gene alteration and protein deficiency in the IHC-tested subset (all four of the four available cases). Among available cases with wild-type MMR but TMB-high, two of three cases were MLH1 deficient by IHC staining, supporting epigenetic silencing and suggesting that the prevalence of MMR deficiency may be underestimated. Reinforcing these findings, MMR-dominant mutational signatures (>50% attributable to MMR-associated signatures) were extracted in eight of 11 cases with genomic or IHC evidence of MLH1 deficiency, but none with the other MMR gene alterations (Supplementary Table 1).

Notably, MLH1 is located at 3p22, between VHL at 3p25 and the chromatin modifying genes (PBRM1, SET2, and BAP1) at 3p21. Since 3p loss is the initiating event in ccRCC tumorigenesis, ccRCC should exhibit near-ubiquitous loss of heterozygosity in MLH1, increasing susceptibility to biallelic inactivation [11]. Indeed, allele-specific copy number analysis confirmed a high prevalence of MLH1 loss of heterozygosity (21/29) and biallelic events (six of nine), whereas this was not the case for the other MMR genes (Supplementary Table 1). Overall, our results demonstrated that MLH1 is the MMR alteration that is most common as well as most reliably predicts protein deficiency in ccRCC, so we focused a subsequent analysis on MLH1.

Eleven patients (2.3%) had genomic or IHC evidence of MLH1 deficiency, and we evaluated the seven with metastatic ccRCC and no other advanced malignancy who received first-line ICIs (Fig. 1B and Supplementary Table 2). All received doublet PD-1/L1-based regimens (of seven, three with CTLA-4 inhibition and four with VEGF inhibition). Five achieved objective radiographic responses, with target lesions shrinking 55–100% and progression-free survival (PFS) of 13–97 mo. Two met the recently proposed Dana-Farber criteria for an exceptional response to an ICI in ccRCC (Supplementary Fig. 2) [12]. Most responders underwent local therapy for subsequent recurrences, but only one received additional systemic therapy (VEGF-targeted second-line therapy followed by successful ICI rechallenge), and all five patients remained alive after 36–106 mo of follow-up.

The hypothesized mechanism of ICI sensitivity in MMR deficiency is increased neoantigen burden [7,12]. While ccRCC generally has a low TMB (median 3.9 mutations/Mb and 2.1% TMB-high across the MSK cohort), most MLH1-deficient cases were TMB-high, with a median of 13.2 mutations/Mb (Fig. 1B). While TMB alone is not predictive of an ICI response in ccRCC, our findings suggest that MLH1 deficiency might impact both the quantity and the quality of mutations, enriching for immunogenic neoantigens, leading to sustained responses [4–6,12]. Interestingly, MMR-deficient mutational signatures were present despite MSIsensor scores indicating microsatellite stability (Fig. 1C). Incongruence between MMR and microsatellite status has been reported in other malignancies, but its significance remains unknown [13].

Our data provide some insight into ICI failure despite MLH1 deficiency. One exceptional responder (ID1) developed a late tumor in the contralateral kidney. Partial nephrectomy and tumor sequencing indicated an MLH1-proficient metastasis from the original primary (Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary Fig. 3), supported by IHC evaluation (Supplementary Fig. 4). This suggests early clonal divergence and subsequent immune escape from tumor heterogeneity, a mechanism known to impair ICI effectiveness in other MMR-deficient malignancies [7]. Meanwhile, one nonresponder (ID4) had a loss-of-function mutation in TAP1. Concomitant deficiency of such key components of antigen presenting machinery (APM; Supplementary Fig. 5) could abrogate any proimmune effect from MLH1 deficiency [14].

We sought to corroborate our findings in independent cohorts, using data from two landmark phase 3 trials of first-line ICI therapy for metastatic ccRCC [1,2]. Among the 427 patients from CheckMate-214 for whom genomic data were available, four (0.9%) harbored MLH1 loss-of-function alterations and were suspected to be MLH1 deficient. Three received nivolumab and ipilimumab, all meeting the criteria for an exceptional response, with target lesions shrinking 76–100% and no progression at 30.6–48.7 mo of follow-up (Fig. 2A and Supplementary Table 2). The fourth received sunitinib and achieved a partial response with rapid progression.

Among the 756 patients from JAVELIN Renal 101 for whom genomic data were available, 34 (4.5%) were suspected to be MLH1 deficient. Eighteen received avelumab and axitinib, with an 18-mo PFS rate of 73.3% (95% confidence interval [CI] 54.0–99.5%) and a 5-yr OS rate of 64.7% (95% CI 45.5–91.9%), after a median follow-up of 74.1 mo among survivors (Fig. 2B and 2C). Notably, eight of 18 (44%) met the criteria for an exceptional response, while three of six with a limited response had coalterations in APM genes (Fig. 2D). In contrast, MLH1-deficient patients who received sunitinib had inferior outcomes with no exceptional responders (Fig. 2B and 2C). The interaction term between the treatment arm and MLH1 status was significant on multivariable regression (hazard ratio 3.71, 95% CI 1.65–8.34, p = 0.001), suggesting that MLH1 deficiency itself is a poor prognostic feature (Supplementary Table 4).

Surprisingly, MLH1 gene alterations did not correlate with RNA expression in the JAVELIN Renal 101 cohort (Fig. 2E). This could be attributable to mechanisms of MMR deficiency: epigenetic silencing correlates more strongly with RNA expression, whereas gene mutation causes end-protein loss of function. Interestingly, three of four patients with wild-type MLH1 but low RNA expression achieved exceptional responses to avelumab and axitinib, again supporting epigenetic silencing and underestimated prevalence (Supplementary Table 2).

While genomic sequencing is not currently the standard practice in ccRCC management due to a limited predictive value, this could evolve as our armamentarium of therapies and understanding of outlier cases broaden. Although IHC remains the benchmark, our study demonstrates that MLH1 deficiency can be identified in ccRCC using genomic data from clinically available sequencing panels. Albeit rare, MLH1 deficiency may represent one of the most reliable predictors of an exceptional response to ICI-based therapy reported for ccRCC to date. While all metastatic patients should receive ICI-based therapy when feasible, future work could explore the implications of MLH1 status for regimen selection, such as combination with CTLA-4 versus VEGF inhibition. Furthermore, while KeyNote-564 marked a substantial breakthrough in the adjuvant space, MLH1 status could be considered in the ongoing efforts to refine patient selection.

In the phase III KEYNOTE-756 trial, patients with high-risk, high grade, early-stage HR + /HER2- breast cancer were randomized to receive chemotherapy plus or minus pembrolizumab9. The pCR rate was signiﬁcantly higher on the pembrolizumab arm (24.3% versus 15.6%; p < 0.01). Finally, in the CheckMate 7FL randomized phase III trial, a similar patient population with high-risk early-stage HR + /HER2- breast cancer were randomized to receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus or minus nivolumab. Results demonstrated a signiﬁcantly higher pCR rate of 24.5% with nivolumab (versus 13.8% with placebo)10. Despite these positive pCR endpoint results in HR + /HER2- breast cancer, many questions remain regarding patient selection for ICIs in the neoadjuvant setting. Notably, in the randomized phase II Gepar- Nuevo trial, patients with early-stage triple-negative breast cancer were randomized to receive neoadjuvant durvalumab or placebo plus chemotherapy. A subset of patients received a two-week window of durvalumab monotherapy or placebo before starting chemotherapy (with or without durvalumab). Among patients in the window cohort, the pCR rate was signiﬁcantly higher for those who received run-in durvalumab versus placebo11. These ﬁndings suggest that the order of administration of chemotherapy versus ICI may be important in the neoadjuvant setting. However, this has not been investigated in patients with HR + /HER2- breast cancer. In this work, to explore the efﬁcacy of chemotherapy plus ICI and understand the biological impacts of an initial chemotherapy versus ICI monotherapy run-in, we conducted a prospective study of neoadjuvant nab-paclitaxel with pembrolizumab in patients with stage II and III HR + /HER2- breast cancer. Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive a two-week window of either nab-paclitaxel or pembrolizumab, with pre- and post-window breast biopsies. Subsequently, all participants received a combination of neoadjuvant nab-paclitaxel and pembrolizumab, followed by assessment of response at surgery. The primary hypothesis of the trial was that we would observe a signiﬁcant increase in PD-L1 expression following initial window treatment with either nab-paclitaxel or pembrolizumab. This hypothesis was based on the premise that either chemotherapy or ICI run-in may enhance antitumor immune activity12–14, thereby priming the tumor microenvironment to respond more favorably to the combination regimen.

Results Patients enrolled and treatment received A total of 32 patients were enrolled between June 2, 2017 and March 9, 2022. The trial was originally designed to enroll 50 patients but was closed early due to slow accrual. Two patients withdrew before receiving study therapy and one was found to be ineligible due to HER2-positivity after receiving one dose of pembrolizumab. The remaining 29 patients were included in the efﬁcacy analyses, and all 30 patients who received at least one dose of study therapy were included in the safety analyses (Fig. 1A shows trial schema and biospecimen collection timepoints/analyses; Supplementary Fig. 1 shows CONSORT diagram). The baseline patient and disease characteristics among all 29 patients in the efﬁcacy analyses are shown in Table 1. The median age was 42 years old (range: 31 to 70). 69% of patients had clinical stage II breast cancer, 72% had clinically node-positive breast cancer, 48% had grade 2 tumors, 41% had grade 3 tumors, and 76% of tumors had pure ductal histology. 17% of tumors (5/29) were categorized as HR lowpositive (HR low + ; see deﬁnition in Table 1); the remainder were HR+. Among the 29 patients in the efﬁcacy analysis, 20 (55%) received all 12 planned doses of neoadjuvant nab-paclitaxel, and an additional 5 patients (17%) received 10-11 doses of neoadjuvant nab-paclitaxel. Reasons for early discontinuation were toxicity (8 patients) and physician decision (1 patient). 48% of patients received all 5 planned doses

of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab, with reasons for early discontinuation being toxicity (12 patients) and physician decision (3 patients; Supplementary Table 1). Additional non-protocol neoadjuvant therapy, which was allowed in case of incomplete clinical response to nabpaclitaxel plus pembrolizumab, was administered to 15 patients (52%), all of whom received 4 cycles of doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide (AC; one with ongoing pembrolizumab; Table 1).

PD-L1 and TILs: landscape and correlation with treatment response The primary objective of the protocol was to characterize changes in PD-L1 expression after treatment with either nab-paclitaxel (Arm A) or pembrolizumab (Arm B) monotherapy, i.e., to evaluate changes in PD- L1 levels between breast biopsy tissue at baseline and at week 3 day 1 (W3D1). It was pre-speciﬁed that PD-L1 expression for the primary endpoint evaluation would be measured by tumor cell H-score, since measures such as PD-L1 Combined Positive Score (CPS) did not exist at the time of trial design. The trial hypothesis was that both nabpaclitaxel and pembrolizumab monotherapy would cause an increase in PD-L1 expression. Twenty-three patients had evaluable PD-L1 scoring at baseline and W3D1 and were therefore included in the primary endpoint calculation (the remaining patients had insufﬁcient and/or unpaired tissue). There was no signiﬁcant change in PD-L1 tumor cell H-score between baseline and W3D1, in either Arm A (chemotherapy ﬁrst) or Arm B (immunotherapy ﬁrst), considering H-score as both a binary and a continuous variable. Speciﬁcally, all patients were PD-L1 negative by H-score (H-score <100) at baseline. At W3D1, one patient (4%; this was a patient in Arm A) had converted to PD-L1 positive (Hscore ≥100; p = 1.00 in both Arm A and Arm B for change in PD-L1 Hscore by McNemar’s test) (Supplementary Table 3). Using PD-L1 CPS in the same calculations, there was again no signiﬁcant change in PD-L1 between baseline and W3D1 in either arm, or in the overall trial population (Supplementary Table 4). PD-L1 CPS and stromal TILs were evaluated on baseline breast biopsies, on-treatment breast biopsies at multiple timepoints (following monotherapy run-in and following combination therapy), and on surgical tissue in patients with residual disease (Fig. 1B, D). At baseline, median PD-L1 CPS was 1 (range 0–100), and median TILs were 7.5% (range 1–90%). Of 26 patients with baseline tissue evaluable for these biomarkers, 18/26 (69%) patients had baseline PD-L1 CPS ≥1, 7/26 (27%) patients had baseline PD-L1 CPS ≥10, and 13/26 (50%) patients had baseline TILs ≥10%. Changes in PD-L1 staining and TIL levels across neoadjuvant timepoints for each evaluable patient are depicted in Fig. 1C, E. There were no obvious visual patterns of change in either biomarker over the course of therapy, with levels starting and remaining low in most patients, though substantial increases and decreases in both PD-L1 and TILs were seen in some patients. Figure 2 shows pCR rates according to baseline PD-L1 CPS. In the overall population, pCR rate was 0% (0/8 patients) among patients with baseline CPS < 1, 28% (5/18 patients) among patients with baseline CPS ≥1, and 43% (3/7 patients) among patients with baseline CPS ≥10. Histologic and biomarker characteristics of the ﬁve patients who experienced pCR on trial are shown in Supplementary Table 5. Three pCR patients were evaluable for BluePrint and MammaPrint (estimating risk of distant recurrence) signatures; all three were basal (Blue- Print) and High2 (MammaPrint).

Safety and tolerability Evaluation of safety and tolerability was a secondary objectives. Among 30 patients who received at least one dose of study therapy, treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) of grade 2 or higher occurred in 97% of patients, and 50% of patients experienced at least one TRAE of grade 3 or higher (Table 3). There were no grade 5 AEs. TRAEs of any grade that occurred in ≥20% of patients were peripheral sensory neuropathy (50% of patients), alopecia (33%), diarrhea (30%), neutrophil count decreased (27%), and fatigue (23%), reﬂecting known toxicities of nab-paclitaxel. The most common immune-related AE was hypothyroidism (in 4 patients, 13%). Grade 3-4 immune-related AEs occurred in 4 patients: pneumonitis (1 patient, grade 4), colitis (2 patients, both grade 3), and alanine aminotransferase increase (1 patient, grade 3). There were no evident differences in toxicity according to treatment arm. A comprehensive listing of all TRAEs, in the overall study population and broken down by arm, is in Supplementary Data 1.

Genomic landscape of the trial population Further biomarker objectives were exploratory. 28 patients had a baseline breast biopsy available for whole exome sequencing (WES) and whole transcriptome sequencing (RNA-Seq). The baseline genomic features of the cohort are summarized in Fig. 3. Individual tumor WES and RNA-Seq data characteristics are detailed in the Supplementary Data Files (Supplementary Data 2 and 3). The most commonly altered individual gene (considering nonsynonymous mutations and indels) was TP53 (12/28 patients, 43%). Common HR+ breast cancer genes GATA3 and PIK3CA were altered in 5/28 (18%) and 4/28 (14%) of patients, respectively. For 14 patients, RNA expression analyses for the MammaPrint and BluePrint signatures were performed at Agendia, Inc, showing 7/14 (50%) luminal B type, 5/14 (36%)basal type, and 2/14 (14%) luminal A type.

Genomic features associated with treatment response and resistance in the overall population To identify genomic features associated with treatment response assessed at surgery, we considered patients with evaluable genomic data and known RCB response on trial, comparing patients with favorable response (RCB 0-I; n = 6 patients) to those with unfavorable response (RCB II-III; n = 20 patients). Of note, this analysis included patients treated with neoadjuvant nab-paclitaxel and pembrolizumab, both with and without neoadjuvant AC. When we excluded patients who received neoadjuvant AC, the top pathways enriched among favorable responders remained consistent with those identiﬁed when considering all patients. We ﬁrst investigated the association between features of the tumor whole exome and treatment response. In an unbiased analysis,

no single-gene nonsynonymous somatic variant was associated with response, which was unsurprising in this small and therefore underpowered cohort. Likewise, there was no signiﬁcant association between TMB, tumor purity, tumor ploidy, or tumor heterogeneity and response (Supplementary Fig. 2). We used gene set and gene signature analysis to identify key biological programs associated with favorable treatment response. Using the Enricher15 program investigating 50 Hallmark oncology genesets, we found that four gene sets (interferon alpha response, interferon gamma response, allograft rejection, and TNF-alpha signaling via NF-kB) were signiﬁcantly enriched in patients with favorable response in the overall population (Fig. 4A). Follow-up single-sample gene set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA), which was performed considering only genes in the four hallmark genesets associated with favorable response in the overall population, similarly showed enrichment of individual genes in the allograft rejection, TNF-alpha signaling via NF-kB, and interferon gamma response signatures among patients with favorable response (Fig. 4B). This further supports a link between interferon gamma response, allograft rejection, and TNF alpha signaling pathways (recovered via ssGSEA analysis herein) and favorable response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab in our overall population. In the converse analysis, we used gene expression data to identify biological programs associated with unfavorable treatment response. The only two Hallmark gene sets signiﬁcantly enriched in patients with unfavorable response were the estrogen response early and late genesets (Fig. 4A). Follow-up ssGSEA, considering genes in the estrogen response early and estrogen response late genesets, showed that higher levels of estrogen response gene expression were signiﬁcantly associated with unfavorable response to treatment (Fig. 4C). Prior work by our group16 and others17 demonstrated that diminished antigen presentation could be one of the immune resistance strategies adopted by tumors with a high estrogen signaling level. Therefore, we sought to explore whether decreased antigen processing and presentation may correlate with higher levels of estrogen response genes in this trial cohort, as well. Consistent with this hypothesis, using ssGSEA, we found a negative correlation (Spearman coefﬁcient −0.41, p = 0.04) between estrogen signaling pathway gene expression and antigen processing/presentation gene expression (Fig. 4D). Moreover, as shown in Fig. 4D, tumors with a favorable response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab tended to cluster with an estrogen signaling-low and antigen processing/presentation-high proﬁle.

Genomic features associated with treatment response by trial arm When the population was broken down by treatment arm, the proﬁles of genesets signiﬁcantly associated with treatment response differed between the two arms (Supplementary Fig. 3). Likewise, when looking at individual genes within the genesets of interest, individual genes that correlated with favorable versus unfavorable response differed between the two arms (Supplementary Fig. 4). Speciﬁcally, genes signiﬁcantly expressed in favorable responders who received initial run-in with nab-paclitaxel were immune checkpoint, antigen presentation, and cell cycle genes, including IDO1, CD274 (encoding PD-L1), antigen peptide transporters (TAP1/2), MHC class I gene HLA-B and MHC class II gene HLA-DRA expressed by antigen-presenting cells, ICAM1 and CXCL10 (known for regulating leukocyte recruitment from circulation to sites of inﬂammation), CDKN2A (which promotes blood vessel endothelial cell migration), and IFNG/STAT1, reﬂecting the enrichment of anti-tumor activities (and nearly all of which are known interferonresponsive transcripts). In contrast, genes signiﬁcantly expressed in favorable responders who received initial run-in with pembrolizumab were genes primarily expressed in immune cells, such as BANK1, CD40, CD8A, and FGL2. These ﬁndings suggest that the immune biology associated with treatment response may differ depending on whether the chemotherapy or the immune checkpoint inhibitor agent is administered ﬁrst.

Discussion In the present study, the combination of neoadjuvant pembrolizumab plus nab-paclitaxel (followed by neoadjuvant AC in some cases) yielded a pCR rate of 17% among patients with early-stage HR + /HER2- breast cancer. While the regimen was overall tolerable and common toxicities mirrored those seen typically with nab-paclitaxel, 4/30 patients (13%) experienced a grade 3-4 immune-related adverse event, and just over half of patients discontinued neoadjuvant pembrolizumab early, mostly for toxicity. Serial on-treatment assessment of PD-L1 and TILs did not reveal signiﬁcant changes in either biomarker following treatment with nabpaclitaxel, pembrolizumab, or the combination. There were many baseline features that correlated with favorable response to the neoadjuvant regimen, including higher PD-L1 CPS and multiple proinﬂammatory immune gene signatures and cell types. The only signiﬁcant gene expression predictor of unfavorable response to the neoadjuvant regimen was higher estrogen signaling. Our cohort’s pCR rate is somewhat lower than the pCR rates recently reported from randomized phase III trials of neoadjuvant ICIs plus chemotherapy in patients with HR + /HER2- breast cancer. In the randomized phase III KEYNOTE-756 trial, the pCR rate was 24.3% among patients treated with neoadjuvant pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy20. In the CheckMate 7FL trial, the pCR rate was 24.5% among patients randomized to receive neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy21. However, all patients on those trials received anthracycline plus taxane chemotherapy, whereas only half of the patients in this trial received neoadjuvant anthracycline. Moreover, the phase III trials almost exclusively enrolled patients with grade III disease, whereas grade III patients only accounted for 41% of participants on our trial. At the same time, chemotherapy is immunogenic in breast cancer12,13, motivating our hypothesis that a chemotherapy run-in could also be biologically beneﬁcial prior to ICI. Though our trial did not show a difference in pCR rates between the chemotherapy-ﬁrst and ICI-ﬁrst arms, we did ﬁnd that the gene sets and individual genes associated with response differed between the two treatment arms. Among patients treated with nab-paclitaxel ﬁrst, favorable responders had enrichment of genes involved in immune checkpoints, antigen presentation, and the cell cycle. In the pembrolizumab run-in group, favorable responders had enrichment of genes primarily expressed in immune cells, such as BANK1, CD40, CD8A, and FGL2. These ﬁndings support the idea that mechanisms of treatment response may differ depending on whether the chemotherapy or the ICI agent is administered ﬁrst, and deserve further investigation in other cohorts. Several studies have suggested that the baseline composition of the intestinal microbiota can affect the response to chemotherapy31,32

and immunotherapy33–37 in solid tumor patients. These effects are likely mediated, at least in part, by the inﬂuence of intestinal microorganisms on the immune system. In a mouse sarcoma model, administration of cyclophosphamide compromised the intestinal epithelium. This allowed the translocation of intestinal bacteria into secondary lymphoid organs, where they enhanced the development and proliferation of anti-tumor immune cells38. In mouse models of HR+ breast cancer, antibiotic-mediated induction of intestinal dysbiosis led to increased levels of intratumorally macrophages and inﬂammatory chemokines, which facilitated dissemination of tumors cells into the circulation39. In our analysis of the gut microbiome, arginine and nucleotide synthesis pathways were the strongest predictors of response to neoadjuvant nab-paclitaxel and pembrolizumab, with lower levels of gut microbial arginine biosynthesis genes, and higher levels of nucleotide biosynthesis genes, corresponding to more favorable RCB scores. One potential biochemical explanation for this association is that lower availability of arginine in the host (due to tumor utilization or immune activation)40 causes compensatory nucleotide biosynthesis from the gut microbiome. Arginine deﬁciency has been previously described in breast cancer cell lines41. The interplay of intestinal microbiota and response to chemo- and immunotherapies in breast cancer remains an area for future research. This study has several limitations. The sample size was small and not all patients had tissue available for all biomarker assessments. Therefore, in genomic analyses, only six patients were in the favorable response (RCB 0-1) subgroup. In genomic analyses, all patients who

received nab-paclitaxel plus immunotherapy were analyzed together, regardless of whether they went on to receive additional neoadjuvant anthracycline. However, sensitivity analyses performed to re-examine key results while excluding patients who received neoadjuvant AC were qualitatively consistent with results of the combined groups. Serial neoadjuvant biopsies (after nab-paclitaxel alone, after pembrolizumab alone, and after the combination) were obtained in all patients and analyzed genomically, including by single-cell RNA technology. These data will offer a unique opportunity to understand the evolution of the tumor and its microenvironment over the course of different neoadjuvant systemic therapies. While those results are not the focus of this manuscript, they have been evaluated in subsequent analyses that incorporate single-cell data alongside the WES and bulk RNA-seq42. We have presented a detailed analysis of tumor-intrinsic and tumor-extrinsic mechanisms of response and resistance to neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus checkpoint inhibition in early-stage HR + / HER2- breast cancer. These results are of high clinical relevance, given multiple recent randomized phase III trials showing improved pCR rates with the addition of neoadjuvant ICI to chemotherapy in this patient population. While long-term follow-up from those trials is still maturing, the results to date suggest that neoadjuvant ICI may become a standard future treatment approach for some HR + /HER2- breast cancer patients. Here we show that more estrogen-driven tumor biology is the major predictor of unfavorable response to neoadjuvant therapy. Conversely, a more inﬂamed tumor microenvironment predicts more favorable response, as has been shown in many other cohorts. We identify decreased antigen processing and presentation as one biological pathway that may underlie the less-inﬂamed microenvironment of strongly estrogen-driven tumors. Ongoing work should continue to dissect the immune biology of HR + /HER2- breast cancer, in order to maximize the clinical beneﬁt of immunotherapy approaches in this common patient population.

Methods Patient population This was a randomized, open-label study that enrolled patients with non-metastatic breast cancer with a primary tumor 2 cm or greater in diameter, with or without nodal involvement. All participants had HR + /HER2- breast cancer (estrogen receptor ≥1% or progesterone receptor ≥1%, and HER2-negative per 2013 American Society of Clinical Oncology / College of American Pathologists (ASCO/CAP) guidelines43). The study (NCT02999477) was approved by the institutional review board of Dana-Farber/Harvard Cancer Center (DF/HCC), and was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Randomization and Treatment Procedures Participants were randomized 1:1 to receive an upfront two-week window of nab-paclitaxel (Arm A) or pembrolizumab (Arm B). The random allocation sequence used for randomization was generated by the study statistician, shared independently with the DF/HCC Ofﬁce of Data Quality, and then implemented via central computer. All study personnel were blinded to the allocation sequence. Patients randomized to Arm A received nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m2 via intravenous (IV) infusion once per week for two weeks. Patients randomized to Arm B received one dose of pembrolizumab 200 mg via IV infusion. After the two-week window, all patients in Arms A and B received weekly nabpaclitaxel 125 mg/m2 in combination with pembrolizumab 200 mg once every 3 weeks, for a total planned neoadjuvant therapy course of 12 doses of weekly nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m2 and 5 doses of pembrolizumab 200 mg administered once every 3 weeks for all patients, regardless of arm. Additional neoadjuvant chemotherapy was allowed at investigator discretion in cases of incomplete clinical response to protocol therapy with nab-paclitaxel plus pembrolizumab.

Collection of research biospecimens All participants underwent a research biopsy of the primary tumor at baseline (within 14 days before the initiation of window monotherapy), just prior to Week 3 Day 1 (W3D1; after the completion of window monotherapy, before the initiation of combination therapy), and just prior to Week 7 Day 1 (W7D1; following 3-4 weeks on combination therapy). Tumor tissue was also collected prior to additional neoadjuvant therapy, for patients who received additional neoadjuvant therapy off-trial (denoted as pre-AC biopsy), and at the time of surgery for research purposes. Stool samples for analysis of the intestinal microbiome were collected from all patients using home-based kits at the following 3 timepoints: baseline; after 1 week of window monotherapy with either nab-paclitaxel or pembrolizumab; and after exposure to both nabpaclitaxel and pembrolizumab combined (Week 4 Day 1).

Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and quantiﬁcation of TILs Formalin-ﬁxed, parafﬁn-embedded (FFPE) tumor slides were prepared and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for evaluation of stromal TILs according to the guidelines published in 2014 by the International TILs Working Group (where stromal TILs percentage is calculated as the area of the stromal compartment occupied by mononuclear inﬂammatory cells, over the total stromal area within the borders of the invasive tumor)44. IHC was performed centrally by Discovery Life Sciences on FFPE tumor samples to evaluate expression of PD-L1 using the 22C3 pharmDx test on the Dako/Agilent Autostainer Link 48 IHC staining platform. PD-L1 was quantiﬁed by (1) tumor cell Hscore, which is the product of the intensity of PD-L1 staining (quanti- ﬁed as 0, 1, 2, or 3, from 0=no staining to 3=strong staining) and the percentage of tumor cells showing positive staining (from 0-100%); and (2) CPS which includes PD-L1 staining on tumor cells and tumorinﬁltrating mononuclear inﬂammatory cells.

Statistical methods The primary endpoint was the change in tumor cell PD-L1 expression by IHC from the baseline biopsy to the W3D1 biopsy, assessed as a dichotomous variable (H-score ≥100 versus 0-99) using an exact McNemar’s test. A key secondary endpoint was the change in PD-L1 expression from the baseline to the W3D1 biopsy as a continuous variable (absolute change in H-score) using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Both tests used a one-sided alpha = 0.05. To achieve 80% power to assess this primary endpoint in each arm (assuming a 20% baseline PD- L1 positivity rate, and 50% post-window PD-L1 positivity rate, and 15% PD-L1 IHC assay failure rate), the trial was originally designed to enroll 50 patients (25 patients per arm) but was closed early due to slow accrual.

Prespeciﬁed clinical efﬁcacy endpoints included pCR (deﬁned as RCB 045), overall response rate (ORR) assessed radiographically by RECIST 1.146, and disease-free survival (DFS). The full trial protocol and statistical analysis plan are supplied as an appendix to this manuscript.

Whole exome sequencing (WES) library construction and sequencing Following similar procedures in our previous study27, an aliquot of genomic DNA (100-250 ng in 50 μL) was used as the input into DNA fragmentation (aka shearing). Shearing was performed acoustically using a Covaris focused-ultrasonicator, targeting 150 bp fragments. Library preparation was carried out using the KAPA HyperPrep Kit with Library Ampliﬁcation (product KK8504) from KAPA Biosystems and duplex UMI adapters from IDT. Unique 8-base dual index sequences embedded within the p5 and p7 primers (purchased from IDT) were added during the PCR process. Enzymatic clean-ups were performed using Beckman Coulter AMPure XP beads, with elution volumes reduced to 30 μL to maximize library concentration. Subsequently, quantiﬁcation was performed using the Invitrogen Quant-It broad-range dsDNA quantiﬁcation assay kit (Thermo Scientiﬁc Catalog: Q33130) with a 1:200 PicoGreen dilution. Each library is then normalized to a concentration of 35 ng/μL using 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0. All steps were performed during the library construction. Quantiﬁcation processes are performed on the Agilent Bravo liquid handling system. Next, hybridization and capture were conducted using the relevant components of IDT’s XGen hybridization and wash kit, following the manufacturer’s suggested protocol with a few modiﬁcations. 12- plex pre-hybridization pools were created by pooling equal volumes of the normalized libraries, Human Cot-1, and IDT XGen blocking oligos. These pre-hybridization pools were then lyophilized using the Biotage SPE-DRY. After lyophilization, custom exome bait from TWIST Biosciences and a hybridization mastermix were added to the lyophilized pool before resuspension. The samples were incubated overnight. Library normalization and hybridization setup were performed on a Hamilton Starlet liquid handling platform, while target capture was carried out on the Agilent Bravo automated platform. Following capture, a PCR was performed to amplify the captured material. Then, the library pools were quantiﬁed using qPCR (automated assay on the Agilent Bravo) with a kit from KAPA Biosystems that includes probes speciﬁc to the ends of the adapters. Based on the qPCR quantiﬁcation results, the pools were normalized using a Hamilton Starlet to the required loading concentration. Up to 24 samples were sequenced per lane on Illumina’s NovaSeq S4 sequencing technology. Cluster ampliﬁcation of library pools was performed according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Illumina) using Exclusion Ampliﬁcation cluster chemistry and NovaSeq S4 ﬂowcells. Flowcells were sequenced on Sequencing-by-Synthesis chemistry for NovaSeq S4 ﬂowcells using paired 151 bp runs.

Whole exome sequences (WES) data analysis WES were captured using Illumina technology. The sequence data processing and analysis were performed using Picard and GATK pipelines on Terra (https://terra.bio/). The Picard pipeline (https:// broadinstitute.github.io/picard/) produced a BAM ﬁle with aligned reads. This includes aligning the GRCh37 human reference sequence using BWA and estimating and recalibrating the base quality score with the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK)47–49. Somatic alterations for tumor samples were called using a customized version of the Getz Lab CGA WES Characterization pipeline developed at the Broad Institute. Brieﬂy, the MuTect v1.1.6 algorithm50 was used to identify somatic mutations. Somatic mutation calls were ﬁltered using a panel of normals (PoN) which was generated by combining normals samples from TCGA51 and the trial cohort. Then oxoG ﬁlter, and an FFPE ﬁlter, was
